subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Proven shortcut formulas for percentages, simple interest, and compound interest. Explanations include derivations, common traps, and speed-comparison vs long method.

questions.stem: What is 7% of 300?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT — SYMMETRY PROPERTY: a% of b = b% of a.
7% of 300 = 300% of 7 = 3×7 = 21.

DERIVATION: a% of b = (a/100)×b = (b/100)×a = b% of a. This is commutative because both equal ab/100.

USE CASE: Whenever one number is a 'round' percentage of 100, swap the roles. 7% of 300 → 300% of 7 = 3×7 = 21 (mental arithmetic in 2 seconds).

questions.stem: What is 14% of 250?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: 14% of 250 = 250% of 14 = 2.5 × 14 = 35.

OR: 10% of 250 = 25; 4% of 250 = 10; total = 35.

BREAKDOWN METHOD: Split 14% into 10% + 4%. 10% of 250 = 25; 4% = 2 × 2% = 2 × 5 = 10. Total = 35. Both methods give 35 in under 5 seconds.

questions.stem: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is:
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: Net change when increased by r% then decreased by r% = −r²/100 = −400/100 = −4%.

DERIVATION: Final = x × 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96x → 4% decrease.
FORMULA: Increase r% then decrease r% → always lose r²/100 %. This is the SAME as the equal profit/loss shortcut — both stem from (1+r/100)(1−r/100) = 1 − r²/10000 < 1.

questions.stem: The price of petrol rises by 25%. By what percent should a family reduce its consumption so that the expenditure remains unchanged?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: If price rises by r%, consumption must fall by r/(100+r) × 100% to keep expenditure constant.
Here r=25: reduction = 25/125 × 100 = 20%.

DERIVATION: Expenditure = Price × Consumption. For constant expenditure: new price × new consumption = old price × old consumption. New consumption = old × (100/125) → reduced by 1 − 100/125 = 25/125 = 20%.

GENERAL: Price rises by r% → cut consumption by r/(100+r) × 100%. If price FALLS by r% → increase consumption by r/(100−r) × 100%.

questions.stem: If 30% of A = 40% of B, what is A:B?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: 30A/100 = 40B/100 → 30A = 40B → A/B = 40/30 = 4/3. So A:B = 4:3.

RULE: If x% of A = y% of B → A:B = y:x (swap the coefficients).

questions.stem: If the population of a town increases by 5% per year, what will be the population after 2 years if the current population is 20,000?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: Compound growth. Population = 20000 × (1.05)² = 20000 × 1.1025 = 22,050.

NET % INCREASE: Net = 5 + 5 + 5×5/100 = 10 + 0.25 = 10.25%. 10.25% of 20000 = 2050. New = 22,050.

TRAP: 22,000 uses simple (non-compound) 10% growth. Population ALWAYS compounds — use (1+r/100)^n formula.

questions.stem: What percent of 2/3 is 4/9?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: (4/9) ÷ (2/3) × 100 = (4/9) × (3/2) × 100 = 12/18 × 100 = 2/3 × 100 = 66.67%.

GENERAL: What % of A is B? = B/A × 100. Dividing fractions: invert and multiply.

questions.stem: At what rate of simple interest will ₹8,000 amount to ₹10,400 in 3 years?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: SI = Amount − Principal = 10400 − 8000 = ₹2,400.
Rate = SI×100/(P×T) = 2400×100/(8000×3) = 240000/24000 = 10%.

FORMULA TRIANGLE: SI = PRT/100. Cover what you want to find:
P = SI×100/(RT); R = SI×100/(PT); T = SI×100/(PR).

questions.stem: A sum doubles itself in 8 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 4 times itself?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: At SI, growth is LINEAR. Double in 8 years → rate R = 100/8 = 12.5% p.a. For 4× the principal: SI needed = 3P (principal + 3P = 4P). Time = 3P×100/(P×R) = 300/12.5 = 24 years.

FAST RULE: Under SI, if a sum doubles in T years, it triples in 2T, quadruples in 3T, n-tuples in (n−1)T years. So 4× = 3T = 24 years.

questions.stem: A sum of ₹12,000 is lent — part at 8% and the rest at 12% SI for 1 year. Total interest earned is ₹1,160. How much was lent at 8%?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT (Alligation on SI rates): If whole ₹12,000 at 8%: SI = ₹960. If whole at 12%: SI = ₹1440. Actual SI = ₹1160. Alligation: distance from 8% side = 1160−960 = 200; from 12% side = 1440−1160 = 280. Ratio = 280:200 = 7:5. Amount at 8% = 12000 × 7/12 = ₹7,000.

ALGEBRA CHECK: Let x at 8%, (12000−x) at 12%. 8x/100 + 12(12000−x)/100 = 1160 → 8x + 144000 − 12x = 116000 → −4x = −28000 → x = ₹7,000 ✓.

questions.stem: The simple interest on ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years is ₹2,000. What is the compound interest for the same principal, rate, and period?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: CI − SI (2 years) = P(r/100)² = 10000 × (10/100)² = 10000 × 0.01 = ₹100. So CI = SI + 100 = 2000 + 100 = ₹2,100.

DERIVATION: SI₂ = 2Pr/100. CI₂ = P[(1+r/100)²−1] = P[2r/100 + r²/10000]. The extra ₹100 = P×r²/10000 = interest on the year-1 interest. This is why CI is always MORE than SI for the same period — the first year's interest itself earns interest in year 2.

questions.stem: At compound interest, a sum doubles in approximately how many years at 12% per annum? (Use Rule of 72)
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT — RULE OF 72: Years to double ≈ 72/r = 72/12 = 6 years.

ACCURACY: Exact answer using (1.12)^n = 2 → n = ln2/ln1.12 = 0.693/0.113 ≈ 6.12 years. Rule of 72 gives 6 — excellent approximation.

PRACTICAL USE: At 8% → doubles in 72/8 = 9 years. At 6% → 12 years. At 10% → 7.2 years. Quick mental benchmark.

questions.stem: At 20% CI p.a., in how many years will ₹1,000 become ₹1,728?

SHORTCUT: A/P = 1728/1000 = (1.2)^n. Check: (1.2)¹=1.2, (1.2)²=1.44, (1.2)³=1.728 ✓. So n=3.

MEMORISE POWERS OF 1.2: 1.2¹=1.2, 1.2²=1.44, 1.2³=1.728, 1.2⁴=2.0736. Examiners use these exact values so recognise 1.728 = (1.2)³ on sight.

questions.stem: A population grows at 10% for 2 years and then declines at 10% for the next 2 years. If the initial population is 1,00,000, what is the final population?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: After +10% for 2 years: P×(1.1)² = P×1.21. After −10% for 2 years: P×1.21×(0.9)² = P×1.21×0.81 = P×0.9801.
Final = 100000×0.9801 = 98,010.

NET% FORMULA: Two +r% rounds then two −r% rounds: net = (1+r/100)²×(1−r/100)² − 1 = [(1−r²/10000)]² − 1. Here: (1−0.01)² = (0.99)² = 0.9801 → 1.99% net loss.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper raises the price of an article by 20% and then gives a discount of 20%. Additionally, he cheats by giving only 900 g instead of 1 kg. His actual profit percent is:
questions.explanation:
STEP 1: Price effect = 20% up then 20% down → net −4% (loses 4% on price alone; SP = 0.96×CP per unit of honest weight).
STEP 2: Weight cheat: gives 900g for 1000g → he actually costs 900g but charges for 1000g. His 'per g' cost is CP/1000; revenue per g = 0.96CP/1000... 

Full calculation: Per kg of goods SOLD, actual cost = 0.9 CP (only 900 g given). Revenue = 0.96 CP (after price adjustment). Profit per 'charged 1 kg' = (0.96CP − 0.9CP)/0.9CP × 100 = 0.06/0.9 × 100 = 6.67%.

SHORTCUT: Net = (1.2×0.8)/(0.9) − 1 = 0.96/0.9 − 1 = 1.0667 − 1 = 6.67% profit.

questions.stem: Find the effective annual rate of interest when the nominal rate is 20% compounded half-yearly.
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: Effective annual rate = (1 + r/2×100)² − 1 when compounded half-yearly. Here r=20%: = (1.1)² − 1 = 1.21 − 1 = 0.21 = 21%.

GENERAL FORMULA: If nominal rate = r%, compounded n times/year: Effective rate = (1+r/100n)ⁿ − 1 expressed as %.

INSIGHT: Compounding more frequently always gives a higher effective rate than the nominal rate. 20% half-yearly > 20% annually.

questions.stem: A sum becomes ₹1,680 in 3 years and ₹1,800 in 4 years at SI. What is the principal?
questions.explanation:
SHORTCUT: SI per year = 1800 − 1680 = ₹120. So in 3 years, SI = 3×120 = ₹360. Principal = 1680 − 360 = ₹1,320.

KEY INSIGHT: Under SI, growth is LINEAR — each year adds the same fixed amount. The 1-year increment = constant SI amount. This lets you back-calculate the principal without knowing the rate.
